name: Valproate (Divalproex, Valproic Acid)
summary: Mood stabilizer and antiseizure medication used mainly for acute mania in bipolar disorder. Powerful but high-risk: carries boxed warnings for liver failure, pancreatitis, and major fetal harm.
description: Valproate (often prescribed as Depakote) is a mood stabilizer and antiseizure medication. In psychiatry, it is used mainly for acute mania and mixed episodes in bipolar disorder, and sometimes for maintenance and migraine prevention. It calms overactive brain circuits by boosting GABA (a calming brain chemical) and modulating sodium channels and gene expression. Because it can cause life-threatening liver failure, pancreatitis, blood problems, and severe birth defects, it should only be used with careful monitoring, and is generally avoided in pregnancy if at all possible.
patient_summary: Valproate (Depakote) is a mood stabilizer that can bring down severe manic symptoms and help keep mood steadier over time. It’s also an antiseizure drug. The trade-off is risk: it can injure the liver or pancreas, change blood counts, cause weight gain and tremor, and has a high risk of serious birth defects and developmental problems if taken during pregnancy. People on valproate need regular blood tests, reliable contraception if pregnancy is possible, and a slow taper if it ever needs to be stopped.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Antimanic Agent; Antiseizure Agent, Miscellaneous; HDAC Inhibitor

linked_conditions.context: Common first-line or second-line option for acute mania and mixed states; often combined with an atypical antipsychotic.
Sometimes used as part of a regimen for bipolar depression, but not a primary antidepressant treatment.
Approved antiseizure medication; seizure control is often relevant for psychiatric patients with comorbid epilepsy.
Approved for absence and other generalized seizures; used when bipolar disorder and epilepsy co-occur.
Approved for migraine prevention but contraindicated for migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy and in people who could become pregnant without effective contraception.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to valproic acid, divalproex, or any component
Active hepatic disease or significant hepatic impairment
Known mitochondrial disorders due to POLG mutations (eg, Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome)
Children <2 years suspected of having POLG-related mitochondrial disease
Use for migraine prophylaxis in pregnant patients
Use for migraine prophylaxis in people of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception

efficacy_response.patient_text: For bipolar disorder, many people respond when total valproate levels are roughly in the 50–125 mcg/mL range, but the "right" level is individualized and based on symptom control and side effects.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally; multiple formulations (IR, DR, ER) with different release profiles.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Extended-release: ~90% relative to IV and delayed-release.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Initial calming of manic symptoms often within several days of reaching therapeutic levels.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Typically 2–4 hours for delayed-release capsules; up to 17 hours for extended-release.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: About 9–19 hours in adults (longer in older adults, shorter in some children).
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism via glucuronidation and mitochondrial beta-oxidation; minor oxidative pathways produce reactive metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily in urine as metabolites; <3% unchanged drug.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Highly protein-bound (~80–90%); free fraction increases with higher doses, low albumin, and kidney or liver impairment.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food may delay absorption but does not significantly change the total amount absorbed.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, valproate is mainly a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder and a backup option for migraine prevention. It is also a broad-spectrum antiseizure medication, which matters for patients with both mood and seizure disorders.
items: {link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar I Disorder – acute mania}: Rapidly reduces manic symptoms such as decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, agitation, and impulsive behavior.
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar I Disorder – mixed episodes}: Helpful when manic and depressive symptoms happen at the same time.
Bipolar maintenance: Often continued after an acute episode to reduce relapse risk, usually combined with other mood stabilizers or antipsychotics.
{link:condition:focal-onset-seizures:Seizure disorders}: Treats focal and generalized seizures; relevant if epilepsy and bipolar disorder coexist.

{link:condition:migraine:Migraine prevention}: Alternative option when other preventive medications fail or are not tolerated; not used in pregnancy or in people who could become pregnant without reliable contraception.
off_label: Adjunctive treatment in bipolar depression as part of a broader regimen
Behavioral dysregulation and impulsive aggression in some neuropsychiatric conditions (evidence mixed; not first-line)
Status migrainosus or severe refractory migraine (IV use in hospital settings)

sections.heading: What People Often Notice
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but common themes among people taking valproate include:

items.category: During Acute Mania (First Days to Weeks)
quotes: The racing thoughts slowed down and I could finally sleep.
I felt less explosive and more able to pause before acting.
Family said I seemed more grounded and less "amped up."
I felt more tired and foggy, especially when my level was high.
My hands had a fine shake when I held a cup.
I noticed my weight creeping up over a few months.
items.note: Sedation, tremor, and weight gain are common and dose-related.

quotes: My mood swings got less extreme, but I had to watch my labs.
It helped stabilize things, but I eventually switched because of weight and labs.
The structure of regular blood tests made me feel closely monitored, which was reassuring.
items.note: For many, the decision to continue valproate is a balance between mood stability and side effects or lab changes.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Valproate doesn’t act as instantly as a sedating antipsychotic, but it can calm mania relatively quickly once blood levels are in the therapeutic range.
key_points: 1–3 days: Sedation and mild calming often noticed as the dose is titrated up.
3–7 days: Many patients start to see meaningful improvement in manic symptoms if serum levels are therapeutic.
2–4 weeks: Full mood-stabilizing effect for acute mania is typically clearer.
Ongoing: Used long term to reduce relapse risk in people who respond and tolerate it.
Half-life 9–19 hours: Allows once- or twice-daily dosing depending on the formulation.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For acute mania, most people who respond to valproate do so when total serum levels are roughly between 50–125 mcg/mL. Some patients respond at lower levels; others need levels at the higher end but may have more side effects. Clinical response and tolerability matter more than hitting a specific number.
sections.clinical_details: Valproate is considered an established treatment for acute mania and mixed episodes and a maintenance option for bipolar I disorder. It is often combined with atypical antipsychotics in severe episodes. Compared to lithium, valproate may act somewhat faster in highly agitated or mixed states, but has greater reproductive and metabolic concerns.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Valproate can cause fatal liver failure, life-threatening pancreatitis, and severe birth defects and neurodevelopmental problems.
sections.black_box: Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity has occurred, most often within the first 6 months and especially in young children and those on multiple antiseizure medications. Life-threatening pancreatitis and major fetal harm (including neural tube defects and decreased IQ) have been reported. Use in pregnancy is restricted to situations where no safer alternative exists.
other: Hepatotoxicity: Early signs can be vague—fatigue, weakness, facial swelling, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, or a sudden loss of seizure control. Liver failure can progress rapidly.
Children <2 years: Markedly higher risk of fatal hepatotoxicity, especially with congenital metabolic disorders, severe seizure disorders, developmental delay, or organic brain disease.
Mitochondrial disease: People with POLG mutations (eg, Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome) have a very high risk of acute liver failure and death; valproate is contraindicated.
Pancreatitis: Can present with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite and may rapidly progress to hemorrhagic or fatal pancreatitis.
Hyperammonemic encephalopathy: Confusion, lethargy, slowed thinking, vomiting, or behavior changes can signal elevated ammonia—with or without liver failure.
Severe skin reactions: Rare but serious reactions like Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and DRESS can occur.
Hematologic effects: Thrombocytopenia and other blood dyscrasias increase bleeding risk and may require dose changes or discontinuation.
Suicidality: Like other antiseizure drugs, valproate has been associated with increased suicidal thoughts and behaviors in a small subset of patients.
patient_counseling: Contact your clinician urgently or go to the ER for severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or loss of appetite—these can be signs of pancreatitis or liver injury.
Watch for yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or intense fatigue—these may signal liver problems.
If you can become pregnant, use reliable contraception and discuss pregnancy plans before or during treatment. Do not stop valproate suddenly on your own.
Report confusion, unusual sleepiness, or sudden worsening of thinking—this can be a sign of high ammonia or other toxicity.
Tell your psychiatrist and primary care clinician about all medications, supplements, and alcohol use—interactions can change valproate levels and risk.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most people notice some combination of sedation, tremor, weight and appetite changes, and gastrointestinal upset. Serious but less common risks include liver failure, pancreatitis, severe skin reactions, major reproductive toxicity, and blood disorders.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness, fatigue, and feeling slowed down
Nausea, stomach upset, diarrhea or constipation
Easy bruising or bleeding (from low platelets)

common.patient_note: You may feel more tired or slowed down, especially during titration or at higher levels. This can sometimes improve over time or with dose adjustments.
A fine shake in the hands is typical. Caffeine, stress, and higher doses make it worse. Sometimes dose reduction or beta-blockers are used to manage it.

common.incidence: Very common (nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea or constipation)
common.patient_note: Taking the medication with food and making slow dose increases can help. Persistent or severe abdominal pain should be treated as urgent.

common.incidence: Common (weight gain in a significant subset)
common.patient_note: Increased appetite and gradual weight gain are frequent. Monitoring weight, diet, and activity early is crucial.

common.incidence: Up to about 1–2 in 10 in some series, often mild
common.patient_note: Can increase bruising or bleeding tendency. Usually reversible with dose reduction or discontinuation; detected on routine blood work.

serious: Acute or progressive liver failure (can be fatal)
Hyperammonemic encephalopathy with confusion, lethargy, or behavior changes
Severe cutaneous reactions: SJS, TEN, and DRESS
Aplastic anemia, neutropenia, and other bone marrow suppression syndromes
Polycystic ovary syndrome, menstrual irregularities, and possible fertility effects
Significant teratogenicity: neural tube defects, craniofacial, cardiac, and limb malformations; lower IQ and increased autism/ADHD risk in exposed children
Reye-like syndrome and mitochondrial toxicity in susceptible individuals

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Valproate interacts with many antiseizure drugs and psychotropics, and can alter or be altered by other medications that affect liver enzymes or protein binding.

items.with: Other antiseizure medications (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital)
items.risk: Complex bidirectional changes in drug levels; higher risk of sedation, liver toxicity, and blood problems.
items.action: Use lower starting doses, monitor levels and side effects closely, and adjust one medication at a time.

items.risk: Valproate significantly increases lamotrigine levels and the risk of serious rash (including SJS/TEN).
items.action: Use much lower lamotrigine starting doses and a slower titration; stop both and seek urgent care if a concerning rash appears.

items.risk: Increased risk of hyperammonemia and encephalopathy, even with normal liver tests.
items.action: Monitor for confusion, lethargy, and vomiting; check ammonia if symptoms appear.

items.risk: Additive sedation and metabolic burden; some combinations may change valproate levels or vice versa.
items.action: Start low, go slow, monitor weight, metabolic labs, and overall sedation.

items.risk: May reduce valproate levels and increase clearance; can also add hepatic stress.
items.action: Monitor levels and clinical response; dose adjustments often required.

items.risk: Valproate can affect platelets and coagulation, increasing bleeding risk.
items.action: Close monitoring of INR/coagulation and clinical signs of bleeding.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression, impaired judgment and coordination; with opioids, increased risk of respiratory depression.
items.action: Limit or avoid alcohol; use the lowest effective doses of sedating medications and monitor closely.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Valproate should not be stopped abruptly unless there is a life-threatening reaction such as severe liver injury, pancreatitis, or a serious rash.
key_points: General rule: Gradually reduce the total daily dose over weeks to months, depending on indication, duration of use, and relapse risk.
Bipolar disorder: A common approach is to decrease by 10–25% every 1–2 weeks while monitoring for early signs of mood destabilization.
Epilepsy: Tapers are often slower (eg, over 2–6 months) to avoid seizure recurrence, especially in patients with prior severe seizures.
Switching to another mood stabilizer: Start and titrate the new medication first when possible, then slowly taper valproate once the new agent is at a therapeutic dose.
Rapid discontinuation: May be necessary for serious hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, or severe hypersensitivity reactions—done under close medical supervision, often in hospital.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Psychiatry-Focused)
sections.text: All doses below are expressed as total daily valproic acid equivalents. Exact dosing must be individualized based on weight, age, comorbid conditions, and co-prescribed medications.

adult.mania_initial: Typical starting doses for acute mania are around 500–750 mg/day orally, divided or as a once-daily extended-release dose, with rapid titration.
adult.mania_titration: Increase by about 250–500 mg/day every 1–3 days based on clinical response and side effects. Some clinicians use a weight-based loading strategy (eg, ~20 mg/kg/day) for faster control in severe mania.
adult.mania_typical: Many adults respond in the 1,000–2,000 mg/day range, but dosing is guided by serum levels (often 50–125 mcg/mL for bipolar disorder) and tolerability.
adult.mania_max: Maximum recommended dose is generally 60 mg/kg/day; doses approaching this require close monitoring.
adult.maintenance: Often similar to the effective acute dose, adjusted downward if possible to minimize side effects while keeping mood stable.
adult.elderly: Start at ~50–60% of the usual adult starting dose (eg, 250–500 mg/day) and titrate more slowly with close monitoring of sedation, gait, nutrition, and labs.

sections.simple_explanation: For mania, clinicians usually start valproate at a moderate dose, increase it every few days, and check blood levels and labs. The "right" dose is the lowest one that keeps mood steady without causing unacceptable side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Because of strong teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks, valproate is a last-resort option in people who could become pregnant.
sections.pregnancy: Valproate is highly teratogenic: it markedly increases the risk of neural tube defects (like spina bifida), other major malformations, and decreased IQ and developmental disorders in exposed children. It should not be used for migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy, and should be avoided for epilepsy or bipolar disorder unless no safer effective alternative exists. If it must be continued, the lowest effective dose and slow-release formulations are preferred, along with high-dose folate and careful perinatal planning.
sections.lactation: Only a small fraction of valproate enters breast milk, and most studies have not shown clear harm, but isolated cases of liver and blood problems in infants have been reported. If a breastfeeding parent continues valproate, the infant should be monitored for jaundice, easy bruising or bleeding, sedation, and appropriate growth and development.
sections.pediatrics: Under age 2, valproate carries a substantially higher risk of fatal hepatotoxicity, especially with neurologic or metabolic disorders or multiple antiseizure medications. In this age group, it is used only when absolutely necessary and with intensive monitoring. In older children and adolescents, seizure and mood indications are individualized, and long-term reproductive and metabolic risks must be considered.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults clear valproate more slowly and are more prone to sedation, falls, and dehydration. Start low, go slow, and monitor cognition, gait, and nutritional status; consider alternatives when recurrent falls or cognitive decline are concerns.
sections.hepatic: Because valproate is hepatically metabolized and can itself injure the liver, it is contraindicated in significant liver disease. In mild impairment where benefits outweigh risks, only the lowest effective dose should be used with frequent monitoring of liver function and free valproate levels when albumin is low.
sections.renal: No automatic dose adjustment is required in kidney impairment, but protein binding is reduced and free valproate levels may be higher than total levels suggest. Monitoring free levels, when available, is helpful in advanced kidney disease or dialysis.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin): at baseline and frequently during the first 6 months, then periodically.
Complete blood count with platelets: baseline and periodically to detect thrombocytopenia or other cytopenias.
Serum valproate levels: check trough levels after dose changes or if toxicity or nonresponse is suspected; consider free levels in hypoalbuminemia or kidney/liver impairment.
Serum ammonia: if there is unexplained lethargy, vomiting, confusion, or behavior change.
Weight, BMI, and metabolic parameters: monitor for weight gain and metabolic complications, especially when combined with antipsychotics.
Pregnancy status: before initiation and at reasonable intervals in people who could become pregnant; ongoing contraception counseling.
Mood and function: track manic, depressive, and mixed symptoms and daily functioning to ensure the medication is helping more than it harms.
Neurologic status: watch for tremor, parkinsonism, cognitive changes, or gait instability.
Signs of hypersensitivity: rash, fever, lymph node swelling, or multi-organ symptoms suggestive of DRESS or SJS/TEN.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Valproate comes in several formulations that differ in release profile and dosing frequency. They are not always interchangeable on a milligram-for-milligram basis.
items: Divalproex delayed-release (DR) tablets: typically taken 2–3 times daily; enteric-coated to reduce stomach upset.
Divalproex extended-release (ER) tablets: once-daily or twice-daily dosing; not bioequivalent to DR on a mg-for-mg basis.
Divalproex delayed-release sprinkle capsules: can be opened and sprinkled on soft food and swallowed without chewing.
Valproic acid immediate-release capsules and oral solution: more rapid absorption but greater risk of GI upset; dosed multiple times daily.
Valproate sodium IV solution: used when oral dosing is temporarily not possible or for certain acute indications in hospital settings.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Valproate works on several levels. It increases levels and activity of GABA, the brain’s main inhibitory (calming) chemical; blocks voltage-gated sodium channels that drive rapid, repetitive firing of neurons; and influences gene expression through histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition. Together, these effects dampen hyperexcitable brain circuits involved in seizures and mood instability.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For bipolar I disorder, valproate is a key option for acute mania and mixed states, often combined with an atypical antipsychotic. It may be preferred over lithium when there is prominent agitation, mixed features, comorbid substance use, or a history of rapid cycling, but avoided when pregnancy is likely or liver disease is present. For maintenance, many patients transition to or combine valproate with other mood stabilizers or antipsychotics based on long-term tolerability, metabolic effects, and reproductive plans. In people of childbearing potential, valproate is increasingly reserved for situations where other treatments have clearly failed or are not acceptable.

seo.title: Valproate (Depakote) for Bipolar Disorder: Uses, Risks, Liver Toxicity & Pregnancy Warnings
seo.description: Valproate (Depakote) as a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder: how it works, dosing for mania, serious risks like liver failure, pancreatitis, and major fetal harm, monitoring, and safer use strategies.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA boxed warnings, major bipolar disorder and epilepsy guidelines, and current literature on reproductive and hepatic safety.

faqs.q: What is valproate used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: Valproate is mainly used as a mood stabilizer for acute mania and mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder, and sometimes for long-term maintenance. It is also an antiseizure drug and an option for migraine prevention in carefully selected patients.

faqs.q: How long does it take for valproate to work for mania?
faqs.a: Some calming and improved sleep may appear within days as the dose is increased. Clear improvement in mania usually emerges over 1–2 weeks once blood levels are in the therapeutic range, with continued gains over several weeks.

faqs.q: Why is valproate so risky in pregnancy?
faqs.a: Valproate strongly increases the risk of serious birth defects, especially neural tube defects like spina bifida, and is linked to lower IQ and higher rates of autism and ADHD in exposed children. Because of this, it is avoided in pregnancy unless no safer effective alternative is available.

faqs.q: What blood tests do I need on valproate?
faqs.a: You’ll typically have liver function tests, a complete blood count with platelets, and valproate levels checked—especially during the first 6 months and when doses change. Your clinician may also check ammonia levels if you develop confusion, severe fatigue, or vomiting.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking valproate?
faqs.a: It’s best to avoid or minimize alcohol. Both alcohol and valproate can affect the liver and nervous system. Together, they increase sedation, coordination problems, and the risk of liver injury.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects I might notice?
faqs.a: Common effects include feeling tired or slowed down, nausea or stomach upset, hand tremor, weight gain, and sometimes hair thinning. Easy bruising can occur if platelets drop. Serious problems like liver failure or pancreatitis are much less common but require urgent attention.

faqs.q: How is valproate different from lithium?
faqs.a: Both are mood stabilizers, but lithium is a simple salt with strong anti-suicide data and more kidney and thyroid concerns, whereas valproate is an antiseizure drug with more liver, metabolic, and reproductive risks. Valproate may work especially well for mixed states and highly irritable or rapid-cycling presentations but is generally avoided in people who could become pregnant.

faqs.q: Can valproate affect fertility or hormones?
faqs.a: Yes. In some people, especially women and people assigned female at birth, it has been linked to menstrual changes, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and possible fertility issues. In men, it has been associated with changes in sperm count and quality in some reports. These risks are part of the decision-making process when choosing a mood stabilizer.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: If it’s only been a few hours, you can usually take the missed dose when you remember. If it’s close to the next scheduled dose, skip the missed one and just take the next dose. Don’t double up without talking to your prescriber, as that can increase side effects.
